```{r setup, include = FALSE}
## Chunks that download public data (several hundred MB) are skipped under R CMD check unless
## NOT_CRAN=true, ie they are not run on CRAN. They run when knitting interactively, with
## devtools::build(), devtools::check() and pkgdown.
online <- Sys.getenv("_R_CHECK_PACKAGE_NAME_") == "" || identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true")
```

# Using credible sets to approximate full coloc

As GWAS and QTL datasets continue to grow in number, it is becoming harder to store complete summary statistics. Organisations like eQTL Catalogue and Open Targets are instead moving to store/make publicly available just the credible   sets at significant loci.

A credible set is defined for coloc as a data.frame() containing at minimum character column snp and a numeric PP column containing the posterior probabilities under a fine mapping. Here we will generate a couple of credible sets from our example data:
```{r load}
library(coloc)
data(coloc_test_data)
attach(coloc_test_data) ## datasets D1, D2, D3 and D4
cs1 <- finemap.abf(D1) |> credible.sets()
cs2 <- finemap.abf(D2) |> credible.sets()
cs1
cs2
```

Now we can compare performing colocalisation using the full data using the usual `coloc.abf()` function or just the credible sets using the new `coloc_pip()` function.

```{r compare}
coloc.abf(D1,D2)
coloc_pip(cs1,cs2)
```

Being able to work with credible sets opens up the chance to rapidly run colocalisation with the large public resources like eQTL Catalogue and Open Targets.

We first generate our own credible set.  Here I'm using one created earlier:

```{r q}
q <- data.frame(chr = 6,
   pos = c(90279406, 90280331, 90281412, 90276601, 90288603, 90286261),
   snp = c("6_90279406_G_C", "6_90280331_G_A", "6_90281412_A_T",
           "6_90276601_A_G", "6_90288603_A_G", "6_90286261_C_G"),
   PP = c(0.675, 0.0747, 0.0702, 0.0505, 0.0422, 0.0412))
```

You will see this credible set has additional chr and pos columns. We will need these to define the lookup region in the public data resources.  The SNP identifiers also have a particular format: chr\_pos\_ref\_alt. This is how snp identifiers are formatted in the public resources, so yours will need to be too in order to match identifiers.

## Set up a cache directory first

Both query functions download files: Open Targets credible sets and a study manifest for `query_ot()`, and eQTL Catalogue files for `query_eqtl_cat()`. coloc keeps these in a *cache directory* and reuses them, so each file is only downloaded once.

Set a cache directory before you start with the `coloc.cache_dir`. You can put this at the top of a script (more reproducible) or put it in your `~/.Rprofile`, so that every coloc session uses it:

```{r cacheopt, eval = FALSE}
options(coloc.cache_dir = "~/data/coloc-cache")
```

If you do not, coloc falls back to a temporary directory with a warning. This works, but the temporary directory is deleted when R exits, so everything is downloaded again in every new session. For this reason, downloads larger than 1 GB (such as downloading all of Open Targets with `ot_fetch()`, or all of several eQTL Catalogue quantification methods with `eqtl_cat_fetch()`) will stop and ask you to set a cache directory.

The options that control downloading are listed in `?coloc-options`:

* `coloc.cache_dir` - where downloaded files are kept (default: unset, so a temporary directory is used, with a warning)
* `coloc.max_temp_download` - the largest download, in bytes, allowed into that temporary directory (default: `1e9`, 1 GB). Set `coloc.cache_dir` to download larger files.
* `coloc.ot_remote` - whether `query_ot()` reads Open Targets files directly from S3 instead of downloading them (default: `FALSE`; see below)

In this vignette we use a cache directory inside R's temporary directory, so that building the vignette leaves no files behind. For your own work, use a directory that persists, as above.

```{r cache}
options(coloc.cache_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "coloc-cache"))
```

`r if (!online) "*The examples below download public data, so they have not been run in this build of the vignette, and their output is not shown. Run them yourself to see the results.*"`

# Query public resources

To query a public resource, you need two steps:

1. `x <- query_*(cs)` will download the data overlapping your credible set

2. `coloc_query(cs, x)` will colocalise your credible set against the downloaded data.

Here are the steps in detail for Open Targets and eQTL Catalogue, in turn.

## Query Open Targets

Open Targets stores its fine-mapped credible sets as 200 files in a public S3 bucket, about 3.2 GB in total for release 26.06. Each file covers a contiguous block of the genome. `query_ot()` works out which file or files overlap your region (usually just one, around 15 MB), downloads only those to the cache directory, and reads them locally. Later queries in the same region reuse the downloaded files, so they are fast and need no network access. It also downloads a study manifest (about 100 MB, once) so it can describe what each Open Targets study relates to.

```{r ot, eval = online}
ot <- query_ot(q)
out <- coloc_query(q, ot)
head(out) 
out[out$PP.H4 > 0 & out$studyType != "gwas",]
```

In this case, we are only interested in seeing what evidence there is for a causal gene, so we exclude studyType="gwas".  We could have done this directly using the type argument:

```{r ot2, eval = online}
ot <- query_ot(q, type="qtl")
out <- coloc_query(q, ot)
out[out$PP.H4 > 0,]
```

## Query eQTL Catalogue

Querying the eQTL Catalogue works the same way as Open Targets. The eQTL Catalogue publishes its fine-mapped credible sets as one large file per quantification method, each covering the whole genome. For coloc, these have been split into smaller files (about 25 MB each) sorted by genomic position, with an index recording which part of the genome each file covers. No credible set is split across files, and the data are otherwise unchanged. `query_eqtl_cat()` uses the index to download only the file(s) overlapping your region - usually one per quantification method - to the cache directory, and reuses them in later queries. 

### Releases and quantification methods

Two eQTL Catalogue releases are available, chosen with the `version` argument: "r8-beta" and "r7" (the default). The split files for each are on Zenodo, for [r7](https://zenodo.org/records/23397994) and [r8-beta](https://zenodo.org/records/23398345). Each release is kept in its own subdirectory of the cache directory, so they never overwrite each other and you can use both side by side.

Within a release, the data are divided by the method used to quantify gene expression, chosen with `quant_method` (default "ge"). You can ask for more than one at once, eg `quant_method = c("ge", "leafcutter")`. See <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/eqtl/Methods/> for details of each method.

| quant_method | what it measures            | r7 credible sets | r8-beta credible sets |
|--------------+-----------------------------+------------------+-----------------------|
| ge           | total gene expression       | 503,000          | 721,000               |
| exon         | exon expression             | 626,000          | 416,000               |
| tx           | transcript usage            | 368,000          | 353,000               |
| txrev        | transcriptional event usage | 411,000          | 403,000               |
| leafcutter   | splicing (LeafCutter)       | 234,000          | 251,000               |
| majiq        | splicing (MAJIQ), new in r8 | -                | 713,000               |

The two releases differ slightly in their columns, and this shows in the annotation of the results: r8-beta credible sets carry a `molecular_trait_object_id` column, while r7 has a `gene_id` column instead.

### Example

We will use "exon" for this vignette. In this case, there is only one exon credible set in the region but it doesn't overlap our credible set and so doesn't colocalise.

```{r ecat, eval = online}
ecat <- query_eqtl_cat(q, quant_method="exon")
out <- coloc_query(q, ecat)
out
```

The same query against the earlier release:

```{r ecat7, eval = online}
ecat7 <- query_eqtl_cat(q, quant_method="exon", version = "r7")
coloc_query(q, ecat7)
```

The credible sets returned contain those of their variants that lie within the query window (the region spanned by your credible set, plus `window` either side, 100 kb by default). Because only overlapping credible sets can colocalise, this rarely matters, but you can increase `window` if you want more of each credible set.

Because ecat is a small object, we can examine its structure. It is a list of credible sets, with an attribute "annot". annot is a data.frame containing one row per credible set giving information about the analysis it refers to.

```{r obj, eval = online}
ecat
```

### Gene symbols

The eQTL Catalogue identifies genes by Ensembl gene id. `ensembl_to_symbol()` translates these to HGNC gene symbols, using the HGNC gene list (downloaded once to the cache directory, about 15 MB):

```{r symbols, eval = online}
annot <- attr(ecat, "annot")
gene_col <- intersect(c("gene_id", "molecular_trait_object_id"), names(annot))[1] # depends on the release
annot$symbol <- ensembl_to_symbol(annot[[gene_col]])
annot[, c("cs_id", gene_col, "symbol")]
```

Ids without an approved HGNC symbol (eg some lncRNAs) are returned as `NA`.

## Downloading data in advance {#downloading-data-in-advance}

Normally you don't need to think about downloading: each query downloads the files it needs to the cache directory, and later queries reuse them. Two functions download data in advance and populate the cache directory:

* `ot_fetch()` downloads all the Open Targets credible sets (200 files, about 3.2 GB for release 26.06).
* `eqtl_cat_fetch()` downloads all the eQTL Catalogue files for the quantification methods and release you choose, plus the dataset metadata. A whole release is about 2.2 GB; "ge" alone is about 0.7 GB.

This is useful when:

* **working on an HPC whose compute nodes have no internet access.** Run the fetch functions once on a login node (or any node with internet access), then run your queries on compute nodes using the same cache directory. The queries find the files already there and never touch the network.
* **running many queries**, so that every region's files are downloaded in one go, rather than piecemeal during the run. See [Many credible sets](#many-credible-sets) below.

```{r fetch, eval = FALSE}
options(coloc.cache_dir = "/shared/project/coloc-cache")   # the same directory you will query from
ot_fetch()                                                # all Open Targets credible sets
eqtl_cat_fetch("ge")                                      # eQTL Catalogue r8-beta, total gene expression
eqtl_cat_fetch(c("ge", "leafcutter"), version = "r7")     # or several methods, from another release
```

Because these downloads are large, they need a persistent cache directory: set `coloc.cache_dir`.

## Multiple credible sets {#many-credible-sets}

Often you will have several index credible sets to test. `query_ot_many()`, `query_eqtl_cat_many()` and `coloc_query_many()` do the same as `query_ot()`, `query_eqtl_cat()` and `coloc_query()`, for a named list of credible sets. They work in two steps: first query, then colocalise.

```{r many, eval = online}
cs_list <- list(locus1 = q, locus2 = q)   # add more credible sets to the list, each named
ot_list <- query_ot_many(cs_list, type = "qtl")
ecat_list <- query_eqtl_cat_many(cs_list, quant_method = "exon")
res <- coloc_query_many(cs_list, ot_list)
head(res)
res_ecat <- coloc_query_many(cs_list, ecat_list)
res_ecat
```

`query_ot_many()` and `query_eqtl_cat_many()` take the same arguments as `query_ot()` and `query_eqtl_cat()`, and return a list of query results, one per credible set, named as `cs_list`. `coloc_query_many()` matches each credible set to its own query results by name, and returns one table of results, with a `query_cs` column first saying which of your credible sets each row refers to.

Keeping the two steps separate means the slow step, querying (which may need to download), can be done once and saved, and the fast step, colocalisation, run or repeated later without the network. For example, on an HPC:

```{r manyhpc, eval = FALSE}
## on a node with internet access
ot_list <- query_ot_many(cs_list)
saveRDS(ot_list, "ot_list.rds")

## later, anywhere
res <- coloc_query_many(cs_list, readRDS("ot_list.rds"))
```

With many credible sets, a few may fail - for example a credible set with variants in a format the query can't use. Rather than stop, the `_many` functions skip a credible set that fails, record why in the "failed" attribute of their result, and carry on:

```{r failed, eval = FALSE}
attr(ot_list, "failed")   # error message for each credible set that failed
attr(res, "failed")       # failures in the query or the colocalisation
```

If several credible sets in a row fail (5 by default, set by `max_fail`), or all of them do, the run stops, as that suggests a problem affecting everything, such as no network access. Warnings - for example about a temporary cache directory, or Open Targets variants on alt/patch contigs - are collected and reported once each at the end, with the names of the credible sets they came from, rather than repeated for every credible set.

The `_many` functions run one credible set after another. To speed up a large run, download the data first with [the fetch functions](#downloading-data-in-advance), so the queries read local files. If you do run queries in parallel yourself, for example with `parallel::mclapply()`, download first in the same way, so that workers don't each download the same files at once. Forked workers (`mclapply()`) inherit your options, but socket-based workers (eg `parallel::parLapply()`, or `future`'s multisession plan) start fresh R sessions without them, so set the cache directory in each worker too, eg `parallel::clusterEvalQ(cl, options(coloc.cache_dir = "/shared/project/coloc-cache"))`.
